item.title: 'General Hospital' star Cameron Mathison says ‘red flags’ drove him to demand answers before cancer diagnosis
item.description: Cameron Mathison opens up to Fox News Digital about kidney cancer, divorce, wildfire loss and how those struggles led him to "A Very Arctic Christmas" with Jill Wagner.
item.content:encoded:
Cameron Mathison knew something was wrong — and spent two years pushing for answers before an MRI revealed he had cancer.

The "General Hospital" star told Fox News Digital the frightening experience changed how he approaches his health, including knowing when to stop pushing his body.

"I just knew something was wrong," said Mathison, who stars in Great American Media's "A Very Arctic Christmas."

'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM

Mathison was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, a type of kidney cancer, in 2019 after an MRI revealed a tumor.

Before his diagnosis, the actor said he had gone to extraordinary lengths to monitor his health, undergoing bloodwork, gut microbiome testing and hormone evaluations. Despite those efforts, he said, troubling results left him searching for an explanation.

"I was a guy trying to do it right, but like I was alluding to, I was very extreme," he said. "And I was doing these extreme things, and I was getting the blood tests, and … things were just off … they were like red flags."

WATCH: CAMERON MATHISON FOUGHT FOR 2 YEARS TO GET LIFE-SAVING MRI

The experience left him with a message for others facing unanswered health questions.

"One of the lessons is to be your own best advocate for your health," he said.

BUSY PHILIPPS DIAGNOSED WITH RARE BRAIN TUMOR AFTER UNDERGOING BODY SCAN HER DOCTOR TOLD HER SHE DIDN'T 'NEED'

Surviving cancer also prompted Mathison to rethink his approach to fitness. After years of pushing himself, he said he now recognizes the importance of rest and recovery.

But his cancer battle was only part of a painful series of losses.

Mathison also faced his mother's death, the end of his 22-year marriage and the loss of his family home in a wildfire. He also lost his hosting job when Hallmark Channel's "Home & Family" was canceled.

'BAYWATCH' STAR NICOLE EGGERT EXPOSES FINANCIAL TOLL OF CANCER BATTLE: 'THE BILLS DON'T STOP'

"In fact, at the time, going through a divorce which was very heartbreaking for me, I had just lost my mom, I had been through my cancer journey, I had all this loss, lost my job, and I was hanging onto that house," he said.

As the losses mounted and his children left for college, Mathison found himself confronting a difficult question about his future.

"And it was like, ‘Now who do you want to be?’"

The actor said those experiences challenged the assumption that making the right choices guarantees decades ahead. Instead, he has found motivation in recognizing how quickly circumstances can change.

"You know, I may not make it home. Like, it sounds depressing, but it's not. It's actually very encouraging and very motivating because you don't know how short life is going to be and to make it meaningful and be kind and loving and compassionate and wise and grateful in every moment is going to make the most of it," he said.

WATCH: CAMERON MATHISON DISHES ON CO-STAR JILL WAGNER'S WILD PRANKSTER SIDE

That appreciation for family helped draw Mathison to "A Very Arctic Christmas," which reunites him with "Lioness" star Jill Wagner.

Mathison plays Jim, a single father and former Major League Baseball player turned broadcaster, whose Arctic cruise with his 20-year-old daughter, Isla, takes an unexpected turn.

A scheduling mix-up leaves the pair stranded after their ship departs without them. They turn to wildlife conservationist Jane, played by Wagner, to help them navigate the frozen wilderness. Maya Rose Skabar plays Isla.

Mathison said the script struck a personal chord because it was inspired in part by his relationship with his children, their travels and the challenges their family has faced in recent years.

"There's a lot of humor in it, there's super, super touching moments in it. There's romance, as we love in a Christmas movie," he said.

He also praised Wagner's sense of humor behind the scenes.

"Jill is such a, sort of like a legend these days, and they see her as this sweet actress in a Christmas movie and then as a hardcore, I want to use a different word, but in ‘Lioness,’ Mathison said. "And … I don't think in any of those roles you get to see her unbelievable sense of humor. She's outrageous and so funny and is the queen of all pranks … She's just so funny, so upbeat, so positive, energizer bunny and obviously just a wealth of talent."

item.title: America's first Muslim senator exposes a political blind spot
item.description: Abdul El-Sayed's election as the first Muslim senator-elect puts Islamism, the Muslim Brotherhood and antisemitism at the heart of a national debate.
item.content:encoded:
As a Muslim woman, physician and longtime critic of Islamism, I have witnessed firsthand the consequences of extremist interpretations of my faith.

I have examined the bodies of Jews murdered by Hamas during the Oct. 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel; recorded the testimony of Yazidi and Kurdish victims of ISIS atrocities in Iraq; interviewed children inducted into ISIS and the Taliban; consoled Christians persecuted in Iraq and Pakistan; and walked through the now-dismantled Al Hol detention camp in Syria.

I know deeply the tragedies promulgated by practitioners of my faith who believe in an extremist interpretation of the religion called Islamism or political Islam. I also know there is a rising tide of people who don’t differentiate between the two and believe all Islam is extremist.

'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS WARN EL-SAYED TO TONE DOWN 'CONDESCENSION' ON MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD QUESTIONS

Islamism and anti-Muslim bigotry took center stage in the midterm elections, which delivered the nation’s first Muslim senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich.

Yet both political parties are challenged in meeting this moment. Republicans too often fail to distinguish Muslims from Islamists, while Democrats seem unwilling to examine the distinction at all. Accusations of "Islamophobia," amplified by the politics of identity and "anti-racism," have further obscured a debate Americans urgently need to have.

Too often, Islamophobia is conflated with anti-Muslim xenophobia to the detriment of Muslim critics of Islamism who seek to expose Islamist influence and to the benefit of Islamist ideology and its allies.

Expect accusations of Islamophobia to be increasingly deployed as a means of diverting scrutiny away from El-Sayed, whose senatorial bid exposed these tensions.

During a television interview, El-Sayed denied that his family was connected to the Muslim Brotherhood. After the election, he joked about the allegations, mocking his critics.

ABDUL EL-SAYED GROWS AGITATED WITH REPORTER AFTER BEING PRESSED ON FAMILY'S ALLEGED MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

Republicans frequently mishandled the issue.

Vice President JD Vance called El-Sayed "very, very evil." President Donald Trump repeatedly labeled him a "jihadist." Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., made sweeping statements questioning Muslims’ fitness for political office. Such attacks risk alienating Muslim voters and undermining legitimate scrutiny of El-Sayed’s political associations, statements and policy positions.

Republicans will continue to struggle with these questions until they understand how Islamism covertly exploits democratic institutions and electoral politics — a challenge identified overseas.

A 2025 French government report on the Muslim Brotherhood examined "Islamist entryism," or Muslim Brotherhood efforts to build influence through local institutions, associations and political structures.

EL-SAYED'S PAST MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD COMMENTS RAISE RED FLAGS AS HE EYES POWERFUL ROLE

Republicans are not alone in their failure to distinguish Islamist political activity from apolitical pluralism.

Too often, Democratic leaders dismiss legitimate questions about Islamist ideology as "Islamophobia," even as disputes over antisemitism, anti-Zionism and the Israel-Hamas conflict deepen divisions within their party.

Following the midterms, former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel faced questions from Fox News host Brian Kilmeade about rising antisemitism and anti-Israel activism within Democratic politics. His responses illustrated the difficulty party leaders face in confronting these divisions.

‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE

Fox News Digital investigative reporter Asra Nomani documented another revealing moment three days after the election, when El-Sayed attended the Arab America Foundation’s national summit where an event leader celebrated El-Sayed’s victory with the declaration, "You destroyed AIPAC twice," before invoking "Free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea."

El-Sayed smiled as these remarks were delivered, without publicly challenging them at that moment.

The phrase "From the river to the sea" is interpreted by many Israelis and Jews as a call for Israel’s elimination, although some Palestinian advocates claim it is a demand for freedom and equal rights.

Such ambiguity makes it all the more important for elected officials to explain what these slogans mean and whether they support Israel’s continued existence as a Jewish state.

JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS

As an expert on Islamism, I can see how such public celebration raises serious questions about the ideological expectations some supporters already place on El-Sayed. He should answer those questions directly.

The same scrutiny should extend to elected officials’ positions on antisemitism, anti-Zionism and American foreign policy toward Israel, Qatar, Turkey and Iran, countries whose relationships with Islamist movements differ substantially but remain important to U.S. national security.

Consider Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., who faced questions during a CNN interview about whether he considered Iran an American adversary. His response deserves examination on its merits, particularly considering reporting about his past statements and associations.

But such scrutiny must be grounded in verifiable evidence, not assumptions based on a politician’s Muslim identity. That distinction is essential.

When all Muslims are portrayed as Islamists, genuine ideological concerns become harder to investigate. When every criticism of political Islam is dismissed as "Islamophobia," the public loses another opportunity for honest debate.

El-Sayed’s campaign offers further examples.

He appeared alongside far-left commentator Hasan Piker, who previously said America "deserved 9/11," a remark Piker later characterized as inappropriate. Piker has also faced criticism over his commentary about Hamas and the Oct. 7 attacks. El-Sayed subsequently distanced himself from Piker.

Politicians shouldn't be held responsible for every statement made by their supporters. But they must be willing to reject extremist rhetoric clearly and consistently, particularly when it comes from influential figures within their own coalitions.

El-Sayed also faced criticism over his "hurt people hurt people" remarks following an attack on Temple Israel synagogue in Michigan that federal authorities investigated as a Hezbollah-inspired act of terrorism — remarks he claims were misconstrued.

Yet political leaders have a responsibility to condemn antisemitic violence unequivocally, without language that could reasonably be interpreted as legitimizing it.

Questions about El-Sayed’s family background and historical associations with Islamist organizations also surfaced during the campaign — allegations involving charities associated with his mother and archived social media statements attributed to his half-sister concerning the Muslim Brotherhood. El-Sayed rejects any claims that he or his family are Muslim Brotherhood affiliates.

More directly relevant are El-Sayed’s published political views. Eitan Fischberger highlighted pro-Islamist 2012 columns co-authored by El-Sayed following Islamist Mohamed Morsi’s election — Egypt’s first democratically elected president, who was ousted in 2013 amid mass protests against his government.

El-Sayed had urged recognition of the Brotherhood’s participation in Egypt’s political uprising.

Those writings are legitimate subjects for scrutiny. Americans deserve to know whether El-Sayed’s views of the Brotherhood have since changed.

MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED

We must distinguish Muslims who support liberal democracy and religious pluralism from those who seek to impose Islamist political principles.

We must also distinguish anti-Muslim hatred, discrimination and violence from legitimate criticism of religiously inspired political movements. The two are not interchangeable.

When politicians conflate them, they create a climate in which ideological scrutiny becomes more difficult and religious prejudice becomes easier to excuse.

Rejecting Islamism isn’t an act of anti-Muslim hatred. For pluralist, anti-Islamist Muslims, it is an affirmation of religious liberty, democratic government, individual rights and the separation of religious authority from state power.

A healthy, liberal democracy must protect the right of Muslims to worship, participate in politics and hold public office while also protecting the right of Americans to scrutinize any political ideology, including Islamism.

El-Sayed should be challenged vigorously on his views of the Muslim Brotherhood, Islamist political movements, antisemitism and Israel’s right to exist. His public appearances, past writings and political alliances provide legitimate starting points for that examination.

Americans must not empower politicians who excuse terrorism, defend antisemitic violence or seek to undermine constitutional democracy, regardless of their religion or political party.

Both parties should support candidates, including Muslim candidates, who defend democratic pluralism and reject political extremism.

The answer to Islamist entryism is neither anti-Muslim prejudice nor silence in the face of extremism. It is informed scrutiny, intellectual honesty and an unwavering commitment to America’s constitutional principles.

item.title: NYC DSA urges AOC to run for president while planning to take over City Council
item.description: NYC's Democratic Socialists of America voted to urge AOC to run for president in 2028, but some resolutions sparked an AI-generated controversy.
item.content:encoded:
The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America overwhelmingly voted to urge Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to run for president in 2028 on Saturday.

NYC-DSA approved a resolution making the call in a 291 to 123 vote at the chapter's annual convention. Gustavo Gordillo, co-chair of the local DSA chapter, said the vote was not a formal endorsement, but is instead a "a commitment to encouraging and building the foundation for a presidential campaign."

"AOC and New York City DSA are committed to building a stronger democratic socialist movement and DSA will create the conditions for a presidential campaign capable of advancing a working-class political agenda," Gordillo said at a press conference on Saturday.

DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA LEADER SAYS ‘MANY’ IN GROUP WOULD BE 'THRILLED' AT AOC IN 2028

The chapter also laid out its plans to take over New York City's City Council, among other resolutions. Several of the party's resolutions ran into controversy for appearing to be AI-generated, according to a report from Politico.

When run through the AI detection tool Pangram, the 2029 City Council election resolution was rated 100% AI-generated, the outlet reported.

Two other DSA resolutions were reportedly flagged as AI-generated as well, related to expanding DSA membership in community boards and interaction with South Asian communities.

The chapter has a policy against AI usage and voted on Saturday to formally oppose the expansion of AI.

NYC-DSA co-chair Grace Mausser pushed back on the accuracy of the Pangram results in a statement to Politico.

AOC CAMPAIGN MEMO FRAMES GROWTH FROM PROGRESSIVE FIREBRAND TO NATIONAL DEMOCRATIC PARTY FORCE

"We are highly skeptical of the results coming out of Pangram as resolutions are often authored and edited in consensus by multiple members," she said, adding that Pangram’s tools "are made by the same industry that’s scraped writers’ work without permission and now sells software to accuse people of not writing their own words," Mausser said.

Pangram claims that its service can correctly identify AI-generated text 9,999 out of 10,000 times. A University of Chicago study also found that Pangram has a near-zero error rate.
